message.content:
The sea doesn’t have a single, fixed color—it looks different depending on a few factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Deeper water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange, yellow) and reflects shorter wavelengths (blue, green). So deeper parts often look blue or even indigo. |
| **Sunlight & Angle** | At sunrise/sunset the light is more red‑shifted, giving the sea a pink or orange tint. Midday, with direct overhead light, it tends to be a clearer blue. |
| **Water Clarity** | Clear water reflects the sky, so it can look very blue or turquoise. Turbid or algae‑rich water can appear greenish or even brownish. |
| **Surface Conditions** | Calm water reflects the sky more, while waves scatter light, making the sea look lighter or more white‑washed. |
| **Substrate** | Underlying sand, rocks, or vegetation can tint the water—dark sand can make it look darker, while green algae can give a green hue. |

So, while we often think of the sea as “blue,” its actual color is a mix of blue, green, turquoise, and sometimes even pink or brown, all depending on the conditions above.
